newsitem.title: INDIA: India's IOC denies borrowing limit hit.
newsitem.headline: India's IOC denies borrowing limit hit.

text.p: Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) on Wednesday denied a newspaper report that the company had exhausted an enhanced $3.5 billion external commercial borrowing (ECB) limit and said there was no danger of its crude purchases being disrupted.
"It is incorrect that we have reached our ECB limit," a spokesman for IOC, which has a monopoly over crude oil imports, said.
Asked if IOC was close to running out of money to pay for crude imports, he replied: "There is no immediate danger of that."

The Business Standard newspaper reported on Wednesday that IOC had told the government it has exhausted its ECB limit, and it would not be able to raise more loans in international markets as its debt/equity ratio had touched two to one.
The report also said the IOC warned that it could lead to a serious disruption of petroleum supplies.
The spokesman said the government owed IOC around 100 billion rupees ($2.79 billion) from the oil pool account deficit. IOC imported more than 30 million tonnes of crude in 1996/7 (April-March).

The oil pool deficit represents money owed to Indian oil companies for selling crude and products below market prices in order to support India's complex cross subsidy system for petroleum products known as the administered pricing mechanism.
The Indian coalition government's steering committee will meet on Sunday to discuss the thorny issue of raising petroleum product prices in order to whittle down the oil pool deficit.
